references.text: The Israelites complained to Moses and Aaron in Egypt, saying that he had made their situation worse, which shows their earlier dissatisfaction with Moses' leadership.
The Israelites would not listen to Moses in Egypt because of their discouragement and harsh slavery, confirming that they had previously expressed resistance against him.
The Israelites complained again, saying they would rather have died in Egypt where they had food than die in the wilderness—the same kind of complaint as at the Red Sea.
The people remembered the food they had in Egypt and longed for it, showing the repeated pattern of wanting to return to Egypt.
The Israelites wanted to choose a leader to return to Egypt, saying it was better to die in Egypt than in the wilderness—the same attitude as at the Red Sea.
Stephen refers to how the fathers would not obey Moses but rejected him and turned their hearts back to Egypt.
Jeremiah 42:14 confirms that fear of war and famine in the wilderness was the same reason for wanting to return to Egypt as in Exodus 14:12.
Numbers 11:18 confirms that the complaint about being better off in Egypt was a recurring reaction to the trials in the wilderness.
Genesis 47:19 shows that even the Egyptians viewed slavery as a survival strategy, providing context for why the Israelites feared dying in the wilderness.
2 Kings 7:4 illustrates the same logic of choosing an uncertain future over certain death, reflecting the people's reasoning in Exodus 14:12.
